analysis.one_liner: Speeds up already-passed credit card and gift card protections so they take effect months earlier.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have moved credit card protections up to December 1, 2009, was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote, dying when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Credit CARD Act of 2009 put new limits on credit card issuers, but most of those protections were set to wait until February 2010 before taking effect. This bill would have moved the major ones to December 1, 2009 instead: limits on interest rate increases, a requirement that penalty fees be reasonable and proportional, and bans on gift card and prepaid card fees. It was introduced in October 2009, sent to the Senate Banking Committee, and never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Credit card holders and gift card users. Issuers spent the months before the CARD Act's effective date raising interest rates and adding fees while they still legally could; this bill would have cut that window by roughly two and a half months, so cardholders facing rate increases and penalty fees in late 2009 would have been protected sooner.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Credit card holders and gift card users

how_it_helps.text: Moves the Credit CARD Act of 2009's general effective date from February 2010 up to December 1, 2009, so its protections apply sooner.
Accelerates to December 1, 2009 the requirement that card issuers review past interest rate increases when deciding whether to reduce a cardholder's APR.
Accelerates to December 1, 2009 the rule that any penalty fee a card issuer imposes — late fees, over-limit fees, and others — must be reasonable and proportional to the violation.
Accelerates to December 1, 2009 the ban on dormancy fees, inactivity fees, and service fees on general-use prepaid cards, certificates, and store gift cards.

analysis.who_pays: Credit card issuers, which would lose the extra months to charge higher interest rates and penalty fees before the protections kicked in, and prepaid card and gift card businesses, which would face the fee bans earlier.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card issuers and gift card sellers

drawbacks.text: The compressed timeline was ambitious: the bill required the Federal Reserve to finish final rules for the fee standards and the APR review requirement by the same December 1, 2009 date, leaving regulators and issuers little runway to get ready, which risks rushed or legally shaky rules.

The gain was real but narrow in scope and time: the protections themselves were already law under the CARD Act; this bill only shortened the interim period by about two and a half months, so it addressed a transitional window rather than a new problem.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For ordinary cardholders the bill offered a straightforward gain: fewer months of rate hikes and penalty fees while issuers waited out the clock. The cost falls on issuers and gift card businesses, whose incentive to charge fees in the interim is exactly what the bill aimed to stop. The main honest criticism is procedural — asking the Federal Reserve to finalize detailed rules by the same accelerated date — but that is a manageable implementation cost against the benefit of protection arriving months sooner.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee the same day in October 2009, no further action was ever recorded, and it died there when the 111th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mark Udall introduced the bill on October 21, 2009.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the day it was introduced.
Thirteen Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
No further action was ever recorded — the committee never reported the bill, and no vote was ever held — and the bill expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit card issuers came out ahead: without a vote, they kept the full interim window to raise interest rates and penalty fees before the already-enacted protections took effect, and cardholders got no accelerated relief from this bill.

for.name: Mark Udall
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on October 21, 2009 to accelerate the CARD Act's effective dates.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill or took any recorded action after referral; the bill died in committee at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll call; on sponsorship the bill was entirely Democratic — Udall and 13 of 58 Senate Democrats cosponsored, with no Republican support recorded.

industries.note: Issuers were raising interest rates and penalty fees in the run-up to the CARD Act's effective date; this bill would have cut that window by roughly two and a half months. The industry's gain from delay came directly at cardholders' expense.

industries.industry: Prepaid card and gift card issuers
industries.note: The bill would have moved up the ban on dormancy, inactivity, and service fees on gift cards and prepaid cards, costing those businesses fee revenue they had planned to collect for months longer.
